kept: A hematopoietic stem cell, also called a hemocytoblast, is the cell from which all the formed elements of blood arise: the red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Hematopoietic stem cells sit in the red bone marrow, the tissue inside bones where blood cells are made.
Unlike embryonic stem cells, hematopoietic stem cells remain throughout adulthood, so new blood cells can keep forming to replace those lost to age or use.
Blood cells arise from hematopoietic stem cells along various paths of differentiation, the process by which cells become specialized in structure and function.
Hemopoiesis, the production of the formed elements, starts when chemical signals called hemopoietic growth factors prompt a hematopoietic stem cell to divide and differentiate.
The division yields two daughter cells: one stays a hematopoietic stem cell so hemopoiesis can continue, while the other becomes one of two more specialized kinds of stem cell.
These two kinds are myeloid stem cells, which produce most formed elements, and lymphoid stem cells, which produce only lymphocytes, a group of white blood cells many of which work in immunity.

CL:0000136|2.label: Adipocyte
kept: An adipocyte, or fat cell, is a cell whose main job is to store fat for later use.
This stored fat holds surplus energy, and adipocytes also help insulate the body.
About half of the body's excess fat is stored in adipocytes in the tissue under the skin, and the rest is stored in adipocytes in other tissues and organs.
Adipocytes make up adipose tissue and store fat as triglycerides, which are lipids, or fats, made of three fatty acid chains attached to glycerol.
Inside an adipocyte, these lipids fill most of the cytoplasm, the material between the cell membrane and the nucleus.
The two basic types of adipocytes hold these lipids differently: white adipocytes store lipids as a single large drop, while brown adipocytes store lipids as many droplets.
Insulin, a hormone released when blood glucose levels are high, stimulates adipocytes to convert glucose to fat.
When blood glucose is low, however, the hormone glucagon stimulates adipocytes to release fatty acids into the blood.
Adipocytes also make leptin, a hormone that reduces hunger; the more body fat a person has, the more leptin circulates.

CL:0000192|2.label: Smooth muscle cell
kept: Smooth muscle cells move food and regulate blood flow in arteries through involuntary movements, which are not under conscious control.
These cells lie in the walls of hollow organs, such as the stomach, intestines, bladder and uterus, and of passageways such as arteries and veins.
Each cell is spindle-shaped, wide in the middle and tapered at both ends like a football, with a single nucleus, and is about 30 to 200 micrometers long.
Inside each cell are thick and thin filaments: the thick filaments are made of the protein myosin, and the thin filaments of the protein actin.
These filaments do not line up inside the cell, so smooth muscle cells show no striations, the bands formed by actin and myosin filaments aligned in parallel.
Smooth muscle contraction can be triggered by hormones, local factors, stretching in some organs, or the autonomic nervous system, which controls heart muscle, smooth muscle and glands.
Inside the cell, contraction begins when calcium ions bind to calmodulin, a protein that aids smooth muscle contraction; this lets myosin heads attach to actin and pull on the thin filaments.
Sliding past the thick filaments, the thin filaments pull on dense bodies, structures fastened to the cell membrane.
The dense bodies then pull on a network of intermediate filaments, protein strands that bear tension, drawing the cell's ends toward its center so the middle bulges in a corkscrew motion.
In single-unit smooth muscle, the cells are joined by gap junctions, channels that let ions pass between neighboring cells, so the muscle contracts as a single unit.

Instead of a macrophage, a monocyte can become a dendritic cell, an immune cell that processes foreign material and presents that material to start an immune response.

Monocytes come from myeloid stem cells, which also give rise to red blood cells and some other white blood cells.

The omentum is a fold of the peritoneum, the membrane that lines the abdominal and pelvic cavity and covers the organs there.
